Before you start

Each slide carries its own point, so you can talk with the room instead of reading notes. Keep it calm and factual; nobody should feel caught. If a student says "I'm hooked," walk them to the nurse or a counselor.

Every student in the room

Some students fear what happens if they ask for help, and menthol and LGBTQ+ marketing were aimed on purpose; every support in the lesson is free.

Slides and notes

Tap any slide to present from there.

Slide 1 · Notes

Open plainly and keep it light: “Today isn’t about who vapes. It’s about how nicotine works, because most of what people say about it is half right.” Nobody in this room should feel caught.

Slide 2 · Notes

2 MINUTES. Start here so nobody walks in thinking vaping is what everyone does. Ask first: “Guess. Out of 100 high schoolers, how many vaped in the last month?” Most rooms guess way high. Then show the slide. Point at the eight puffs: “That’s it. Eight.”

Slide 3 · Notes

5 MINUTES. Read each one. Stand for fact, stay seated for myth. Don’t reveal yet; just notice where the room splits. Option: hand the reading to a student.

Slide 4 · Notes

Point at the one the room split on most. On #1, don’t explain yet: “We’re coming back to that one, because it’s the sneakiest.” If someone says vapes are less bad than cigarettes, agree. That’s true for an adult smoker who switches, and admitting it buys you credibility for everything else.

Slide 5 · Notes

3 MINUTES. Nicotine fits receptors your brain already has and makes dopamine neurons fire within seconds. Dopamine’s job is to mark “do that again,” and it marks the setting too: the bathroom, the car, the friend, the after-school slump. Later those places start the craving by themselves. Ask: “Ever walk into a kitchen and suddenly want a snack you weren’t thinking about?” Same idea.

Slide 6 · Notes

4 MINUTES. Walk the loop with your finger on the screen: a cue, the hit, the relief, it wears off, the craving, and the next cue lands harder. With regular use the brain adds nicotine receptors and needs nicotine to feel normal. The brakes, the part of the brain that says “wait,” keep building into the mid-20s, which is part of why teens get hooked faster than adults.

Slide 7 · Notes

1 MINUTE. Tell a short true one of your own: a time you tried to give up coffee, your phone, sugar, anything. What was the cue? What did the craving feel like? Did you slip? Keep it light. The point is that everybody has a loop, so nobody in the room is the problem. Then: “Now picture that, but with a chemical that sets off dopamine in seconds.”

Slide 8 · Notes

2 MINUTES. Turn and talk, then take a few shouted answers from the room. Expect: between classes, the bathroom, before a test, in the car, after a fight, bored. The point: the cue is part of the habit, so any plan to quit has to cover the cue too.

Slide 9 · Notes

5 MINUTES. This is the idea most worth leaving with. Point to the hole: as nicotine wears off you feel edgy and foggy. The next hit climbs you back to normal, which is where the kid on the left already is. The relief is real; the stress was mostly withdrawal. Ask: “Why would that make it hard to quit?” Let them get there: quitting feels like losing your stress relief.

Slide 10 · Notes

3 MINUTES. Groups talk through this one, then report back. Next slide shows the answer.

Slide 11 · Notes

The answer, once the room has had its say.

Slide 12 · Notes

3 MINUTES. Groups talk it through, then click to show the point. Pouches skip the lungs, which is real. They don’t skip the brain: same nicotine, same cue, hit, relief, craving. Switching products isn’t the same as quitting. Next slide shows the answer.

Slide 13 · Notes

The answer, once the room has had its say.

Slide 14 · Notes

3 MINUTES. Keep this one respectful of parents. Families draw this line differently, and some students live with smoking as normal. Next slide shows the answer.

Slide 15 · Notes

The answer, once the room has had its say.

Slide 16 · Notes

4 MINUTES. If students like data: in a 2024 trial of 1,503 teens, 37.8% using the text program had quit seven months later, versus 28.0% without it. Also cover helping a friend: don’t lecture, offer to walk with them to the nurse, and back them up when they say “I’m quitting.”

Slide 17 · Notes

5 MINUTES. Read the top line and let it sit. Then the exit card: anonymous, one answer, collected face down. Share the take-home link after class; it has the loop, the quit steps, and who to talk to, including after hours.

If you want more

The full plan, care notes, and research. None of it is needed to teach the lesson.

Lesson plan

A suggested plan. Change the timing, skip or reorder slides, or use any part on its own. You know your students.

Goal

Students can explain how nicotine dependence builds (cue, hit, relief, craving), why vaping feels like stress relief, and name two real ways to get help quitting. The aim is understanding. Nobody in the room should feel caught.

Materials

  • The deck on the big screen. Each slide carries its own point, so no script is needed.
  • The take-home link to share after the talk

Flow

  1. 5 minThe real number (92 of 100 didn’t vape) and myth or fact
  2. 8 minHow it hooks: the brain stamps it, the loop, a quick story
  3. 8 minCues, then the stress trap
  4. 9 minThree moments, one per slide
  5. 5 minQuitting is a skill, the closing line, one question to answer

Short on time (20-minute advisory)

The real number, myth or fact, the loop, the stress trap, one of the three moments, and the closing slide. Share the take-home link afterward.

Before you teach
Assume all four groups are in the room.

Students who have never tried it, students who vape now and then, students who are dependent, and students whose parent smokes or vapes. Talk to all four. Don't ask for a show of hands about anyone's use.

Keep it factual and calm.

Teens tune out exaggeration fast, and one overstated claim can cost you the rest of the period. The real facts are strong enough on their own.

If a student says "I'm hooked."

Thank them and say you want to get them help, not get them in trouble. Walk them to the nurse or a counselor that day.

Watch the family angle.

"Your dad's choice and your choice are different decisions" respects the family. Avoid anything that makes a parent sound foolish. Some students are worried about that parent.

THC comes up. Let it.

Students may ask about weed carts. The lung injury outbreak (EVALI) was mostly tied to THC carts from informal sellers. Stick to that fact, and offer the weed lesson if your school uses it.

If someone gets sick after vaping.

Trouble breathing, chest pain, confusion or passing out is a 911 call. Poison Control is 1-800-222-1222. Vape liquid swallowed by a small child is poisonous.

Every student in the room

Culture, family, identity, ability and money: what to keep in mind for this topic.

Families draw different lines.

In some homes smoking or vaping is an ordinary adult habit, sometimes tied to culture or community. In others any nicotine is off limits. Teach it as health information, never as a judgment of anyone's family.

Marketing has aimed at some groups on purpose.

Tobacco companies have long marketed menthol heavily in Black communities, and have run campaigns aimed at LGBTQ+ young people. Naming that helps students see the target, not blame each other.

Disclosure feels riskier for some students.

Students from families or communities with more experience of discipline or police may fear what happens if they say "I'm hooked." Say plainly what happens next at your school.

Some students say it helps them focus.

Students with ADHD or anxiety sometimes describe vaping as self-medication. Take that seriously and connect them with the nurse or a counselor rather than debating it in front of the class.

Cost and language.

Every support in this lesson is free (the text program, the nurse, a counselor). Some students translate health information for their family; the take-home sheet is written in plain language they can share.

Who "family" is.

The parent scenario works with any adult at home: a grandparent, an aunt, a foster parent. Swap in whoever fits your students.

What the research says

In 2024, 7.8% of U.S. high school students had vaped in the past 30 days, the lowest in a decade. Nicotine pouches were the second most used product.

National Youth Tobacco Survey, 2024 (Jamal et al., MMWR)

Nicotine makes dopamine neurons fire in bursts within seconds. With regular use the brain adds nicotine receptors and needs nicotine to feel normal. Attention and impulse-control circuits are still maturing into the mid-20s.

Surgeon General's report on youth e-cigarette use, 2016

Nicotine doesn't lower stress overall. Dependent users feel tense as it wears off, and the next dose brings them back to where non-users already are. People who quit report less stress over time.

Parrott, American Psychologist, 1999

In a study of 681 seventh graders in central Massachusetts, 22% of those who smoked occasionally reported a dependence symptom within four weeks of starting monthly use.

DiFranza et al., Tobacco Control, 2000

Substantial evidence that e-cigarette use raises the risk that young people try cigarettes. Conclusive evidence that vape aerosol has fewer toxicants than cigarette smoke, which matters for an adult smoker who switches completely.

National Academies of Sciences, 2018

2,807 hospitalizations and 68 deaths from EVALI in 2019 and 2020, mostly tied to vitamin E acetate in THC carts.

CDC, final update, February 2020

In a trial with 1,503 teens who vaped, 37.8% using the This is Quitting text program had stopped seven months later, compared with 28.0% without it.

Graham et al., JAMA, 2024

Massachusetts raised the buying age to 21 in 2018 and banned flavored vapes in 2019. Flavored disposables still arrive through illegal imports, often with no reliable label.
